WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Balika Samridhi Yojana 
*381. SHRI DWIJENDR A NATH SHARMAH: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the aims and objectives of the Balika Samridhi Yojana; and 
(b) the details of the amount allocated and released to Assam under this 
scheme during the last three years, year-wise and district-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) Scheme called 'Balika Samridhi Yojana' a 100% 
4 

[23 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme aims to provide benefits for the girl child. The 
objectives of the scheme are— 
(i) To change the negative family and community attitude towards the 
girl child at birth and towards her mother. 
(ii) To improve enrollment and retention of girl children in schools. 
(iii) To raise the age at marriage of girls. 
(iv) To assist the girl to undertake income generating activities. 
The scheme was formally launched on 2nd October, 1997 and recast in 1999. 
However in the year 2001 the Planning Commission decided that the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme Balika Samridhi Yoja na should be transferred to States. 
This decision could not be formally confirmed by the National Development 
Council. In the mean time because of non-receipt of Utilisation Certificates, 
funds were not released to the States running the scheme. Now the Department 
has decided to release funds to those States that have now submitted 
satisfactory Utilisation Certificates. F unds will be released after making 
provision in the Revised Estimates under this Head. 
(b) Since inception of the scheme in 1997, Rs. 594.02 lakhs has been 
released to Assam. So far State Government of Assam has submitted 
utilisation certificates only for Rs. 436.94 lakhs. Due to unspent balance of Rs. 
157.08 lakhs with the State, no funds have been released to the Government of 
Assam during the last three financial years. 
Children's Film Festival 
*382. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of cities hosting children's film festival since 1995; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Hyderabad has become a prominent centre 
for hosting the International Children's Film Festival; 
(c) if so, whether Government find any justification in establishing a 
children's film festival complex at Hyderabad; 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2004] 
(d) if so, whether Government have initiated any move in this 
direction; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Since 1995, the International Children's Film 
Festival has been organized at Hyderabad in collaboration with the Government 
of Andhra Pradesh, once every two years. 
(b) to (e) In the year 1997, Hydera bad was declared as the permanent 
venue for the International Children's Film Festival. The land handed over to 
Children's Film Society, India (CFSI) in 1997, for the Children's Film 
Complex had to be surrendered on account of non receipt of permission for 
'change of land use' and opposition from heritage conservationists. Later, while 
the proposal of construction of the Complex was still under consideration (at 
different levels), the Expenditure Reforms Commission (ERC) recommended the 
winding up of CFSI itself. Under these circumstances, the large capital 
investment required for setting up a complete festival complex with offices and 
theatres for a festival held for a duration of seven days every two years was 
not found feasible. Based on this, the scheme was taken out from the Schemes 
for the Tenth Five Year Plan. However, a proposal to revive the project of 
construction of a complex at Hyderabad is again under serious consideration 
of the Ministry.

Basic minimum infrastructure in schools 
*389. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the existing school system is deeply flawed in its inability to 
secure safety of the school going children; 
(b) by when the country would get rid of crowded classrooms with 
inflammable roofing, poor access, no exits, primitiv e kitchen facilities and at 
times without drinking water or toilet facilities in the schools; and 
(c) the steps proposed to ensure the basic minimum infrastructure in 
order to prevent deaths of students? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) The Ministry of Human Resource Development is 
deeply concerned about the status of infr astructure facilities and safety of the 
school children. The tragedy involving the death of 94 children at an Aided 
Private School at Kumbakonam in Tamil Nadu has highlighted the need for 
effective fire protection. 
A preliminary assessment was carried out for Central Government 
Schools to find out the status of fire protection equipment and measures. Many 
of the Kendriya Vidyalayas (KVs) were found wanting in fire protection 
equipment; Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas (JNVs), however, enjoyed better 
infrastructure facilities including fire protection equipment. 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2004] 
Detailed instructions have now been issued for providing adequate fire safety 
measures in all Central Government Schools within three months. KVs and 
JNVs running in temporary buildings have been specially targeted; school-
wise survey will be conducted there, estimates made for additional facilities and 
adequate health and safety measures provided within three months. The 
campaign will be monitored on weekly basis. 
Further, as most of the primary and secondary schools are in the State 
Sector, the Minister of Human Resource Development has written to all the 
Chief Ministers and Union Territory Ad ministrators to provide 'personal 
leadership & direction in ensuring health and safety of school children'. Copy 
enclosed as Statement (See below). 
Sixteenth July every year has been suggested for observing as "School 
Health and Safety Day" in all the schools when safety drills and other activities 
will be organised for inculcating appropriate health and safety culture among 
teachers and students.

AND INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to (b) the 
Government has a two-pronged strategy for dealing with the negotiations in the 
WTO including the on-going negotiations under the Doha Work Programme 
and those relating to adoption of the Framework Agreement by the General 
Council on 1st August, 2004 setting the roadmap for these negotiations. On the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) There was a decline in 
the demand for Indian tea in the international market during the last few years. 
However, during the first quarter of the current financial year 2004-05, tea 
exports from India were higher at 41 .46 million kgs. as compared to 30.23 
million kgs. during the corresponding period of 2003-04. 
(b) and (c) The Indian tea industry has been passing through a period of 
depressed prices over the past five years. This continuous fall in prices of tea, 
coupled with high costs of production, sluggish rate of growth of domestic 
demand and fall in exports have adversely affected the viability of tea gardens, 
particularly the medium sized and financially weak, resulting in 
closure/abandonment of some tea gardens in the country. The industry is also 
beset with long term problems like old age of the plantations, worn-out 
machinery in the processing factories and poor infrastructure facilities.

condition of the Indian tea industry. These include setting up of a special 
fund equivalent to collections by way of additional duty of excise

have been re-oriented with this objective. Tea Board is also implementing a 
new scheme of Quality Upgradation and Product Diversification during the 
Tenth Plan period under which subsidy is provided for modernization of the 
processing factories etc. For productivity improvement, subsidy is being provided 
by the Tea Board for renovation of old tea bushes by way of replanting, 
replacement planting, rejuvenation pruning and Consolidation through in filling, 
creation of irrigation facilities etc. Tea Board is also orgainsing training 
programmes for imparting training on quality and productivity improvement 
measures to both small and large growers. The import duty on items of machinery 
used to improve productivity and quality of tea, including value addition, has been

Differences between WTO Member countries 
1960. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHAR YA: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the member countries of the WTO are sharply divided over 
further reforms and liberalisation of agriculture particularly on the nature and 
extent of reduction in trade-distorting domestic support and improvements in 
market access; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) to what extent these differences have been ironed out in the Geneva 
Conference and in what manner and subject to what conditions the interests of 
agriculture sector of the developing countries have been protected? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) In the ongoing 
negotiations on the world Trade Organisation (WTO) Agreement on 
Agriculture, development Members have been calling for substantial reductions 
in trade-distorting domestic support and elimination by a credible end date of 
all forms of export subsidies by developed countries and substantial 
improvements in market access consistent with the Doha mandate on agriculture. 
Developed countries, in turn, have been wanting to lower the ambition in the 
required reform of their agricultural sector, 
52 

[23 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
while at the same time calling for commitments from developing countries, in 
particular in market access, which were not consistent with developing country 
rural development, food security and livelihood security needs. 
(c) The General Council of the WTO adopted on 1 August 2004 by 
consensus of all its Members, a Decision on the Doha Work Programme 
incorporating also a Framework for Establishing Modalities in Agriculture. The 
agreed Framework duly addresses, without any conditions, the interests and 
concerns of India. It contains elements and principles based on which modalities 
will be negotiated for substantial overall reduction in trade-distorting domestic 
support using a tiered formula with Members with higher levels of such support 
making deeper cuts, along with separate disciplines on each of its sub-
components. All forms of export subsidies will be eliminated by a creadible end 
date, and substantial improvements in market access of developed countries will 
be achieved through a tiered formula with higher tariffs attracting deeper cuts. In 
respect of developing countries, the tariff reduction formula, number and 
treatment of sensitive products, and any expansion in tariff rate quotas has 
been made contingent upon their food security, livelihood security and rural 
development needs being met. Proportionality through lower tariff reduction 
commitments and tariff rate quota commitments by developing c ountries as 
compared to those by developed countries has been explicitly incorporated. An 
appropriate number of Special Products with flexibility in treatment based on 
criteria as agreed in the Framework of food security, livelihood security and rural 
development of developing countries ha ve also been agreed along with 
institution of a new Special Safeguard Mechanism. Developing countries 
shall have the flexibility to provide marketing and transport subsidies on 
exports for a reasonable period beyond the elimination of all export subsidies, 
and those like India that allocate almost all de minimis support to subsistence 
and resource poor farmers shall be exempted from reducing such support. 
Special and differential treatment for developing countries, including longer 
implementation periods, shall be integral to all aspects of the negotiations.

1972. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of CULTURE be pelased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the United Nations Educational, Scientific 
61 
 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2004] 
and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) has declared the Brihadisvara temple 
of Tangaikondadilapuram in Permabadur district  and the Airavatesvara 
temple of Darasuram in Thanjavur district as World Heritage Monuments; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government had requested the UNESCO to declare more 
monuments in the country as World Heritage; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) According to norms laid down by the World Heritage Committee 
each member state can propose for inclusion of similar sites having 
outstanding universal value as an extension to the site already inscribed 
on the World Heritage List. Accordingly, both the temples i.e. the 
Brihadisvara temple at Gangaikondacholapuram and the airavatesvara 
temple at Darasuram have been inscribed as an extension to the 
Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur under criteria i, ii, iii, and iv. 
As per criteria (i), all the three Chola temples represent an 
outstanding creative achievement in architectural conception of dravida 
type. Under criteria (ii), temples bear witness to development from the 
first great temple at Thanjavur. The crit eria (iii), describes the three Chola 
temples as an exceptional and the most outstanding testimony of the 
development of the architecture of the Chola Empire. Criteria (iv), marks 
all the three temples as outstanding  examples of the architecture and 
the representation of the Chola ideology.  
(c) yes, Sir. 
(d) As per decision taken by the World Heritage Committee in the 24th 
session held at Cairn (Australia) each member state can propose only one new 
nomination per year for inclusion in th e list. From India, nomination dossier 
for Sri Harimandir Sahib (Golden Temple), Amritsar for the year 2005 and 
Majuli Island, Assam for 2006 have already been submitted to the World 
Heritage Centre.

No.PS/DE/2004/10496-11595 Dated: 27/4/04 
ORDER 
Whereas in CWP No. 3156 of 2002, the Hon'ble Delhi High Court has 
directed the Directorate of Education to frame appropriate rules to ensure that 
children of weaker sections of the society are given freeship in Recognised 
Unaided Schools; 
And Whereas it is necessary to issue orders in this regard directing all the 
Recognised Unaided Schools to grant freeship to the Children of economically 
weaker sections in such schools. 
Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred on me under section 
3(1) of the Delhi School Education Act, 1973 read with Rule 43 of the Delhi 
School Education Rules, 1973, I Rajendra Kumar, Director of Education, 
Government of NCT of Delhi do hereby order the following:—

Tution Fees, PTA or any other fe es/funds/charges of any kind

sections of society w.e.f. 1st May, 2004.

Statement 
Certificate Course in Watershed Technology/Management 
Earth System: 
Earth as a member of solar family. Atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere. 
Idea about the age and interior of the earth. 
Weather and Climate: 
Latitudes and longitudes. Weather and climate, atmospheric general circulation. Air 
mass as weather fronts. Weather elements. Monsoon circulation, types of rainfall 
distribution. Monsoon through monsoon depressions and tropical cyclones. 
Recording of rainfall, rain gauge, methods of determining mean areal depth of rainfall. 
Introductory Geology: 
Geological Time Scale. A brief history of the earth through geological time. Rocks as 
agreegates of minerals, types of rocks. Main geological formations of India as water 
bearing strata. 
Weathering and erosion. Soil formation, soil profile and classification of soils. 
Rocks as layers (beds), their attitude (dip and strike) Use of clinometer 
compass and Brunton compass. Simple geological structures: Folds, faults and 
unconformities. 
Maps: Topographical maps, scale and its representation. Map reading. Global 
Positioning System (GPS) and its use. 
Geological agents, their erosional and depositional activities. Brief introduction to 
types of land forms. Study of toposheets: Land forms drainage patters and 
watershed. 
Water Resources: Hydrological cycle. Assessment of surface and groundwater 
resources. National water resources. Economics of water use, legal control of water use. 
Need for sustainable water management. NGOs and their role in water management 
practices. 
Ground Water: 
Occurrence, Vertical distribution of ground water. Aquifers, confined and 
unconfined. Water table variations. Perched water table. Porosity 
106 

[23 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
and permeability. Movement of ground wate r, Darc/s Law. Types of wells. 
Introductory ideas about the following: Water logging, Conjunctive use of water; 
Causes for depletion of water table. Water analysis kit and its use. Elementory 
idea about groundwater exploration. 
Water Quality: 
Physical, chemical and biological characteristics of water, their 
significance. Standards for drinking and agriculture water. 
Pollution of water: Water pollutants, sources and remedial measures. 
Fluoride and arsenic problems in ground water. Graphical presentation 
of chemical data and its interpretation. 
Watershed: 
Definition, significance principles and objectives. Watershed 
characteristics, causes of deterioration. Principal factors 
influencing watershed operation. Introduction to watershed 
hydrology. 
Water Conservation: 
Introductory ideas: 
Conservation measures: Gully control, terracing, bunding, check dams; 
reclamation of soils. Afforestation. 
Water Harvesting. Rain water harvesting, roof water harvesting, 
artificial recharge. 
Practicals: 
Mean areal depth of rainfall by Theissen polygons and by Isoheytal 
methods.

[23 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and 
(b) According to the 2001 census, the literacy rate in the country was 64.8%. 
Kerala has the highest literacy rate and Bihar has the lowest literacy rate in 
the country. 
(c) The universalisation of elementary education and eradication of adult 
illiteracy form the two-pronged strategy for improving the literacy rate of the 
country. In the elementary education sector, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) has 
been launched with a holistic and convergent approach to implement 
Universalisation of Elementary Education in a mission mode with the district 
focus. The goals of SSA are:- 
• All Children in School, Education Guarantee Centre, Alternate 
School, 'Back-to-School' camp by 2003. 
• All children complete five years of primary schooling by 2007. 
• All children complete eight years of elementary schooling by 2010. 
• Focus on elementary education for satisfactory quality with 
emphasis on education for life. 
• Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 2007 
and at elementary education level by 2010. 
• Universal retention by 2010. 
The National Literacy Mission (NLM) aims to provide functional 
literacy to non-literates in 15—35 age group. The thrust areas of NLM are 
improving female literacy in low female literacy areas, to organize residual 
illiteracy projects in areas, which have substantial number of illiterates, and 
to set up continuing education centres for providing opportunities for life long 
learning to the neo-literates.

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2004] 
Statement 
Proposal for checking the entry of criminals in Parties 
Criminalisation of politics 
This is an issue being raised by the Commission from 1998 onwards. 
Disqualification for criminal offences is provided for in Section 8 of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951. As per that Section, a person is 
disqualified from contesting election only on conviction by the Court of Law. 
There have been several instances of persons charged with serious and heinous 
crimes like murder, rape, dacoity, etc. contesting election, pending their trial, 
and even getting elected in a large number of cases. This leads to a very 
undesirable and embarrassing situation of law breakers becoming law makers 
and moving around under police protection. 
The Commission had proposed that the law should be amended to provide 
that any person who is accused of an offence punishable by imprisonment for 
five years or more should be disqualified from contesting election even when trial 
is pending, provided charges have been framed against him by the competent 
court. The Commission reiterates that such a step would go a long way in 
cleansing the political establishment from the influence of criminal elements 
and protecting the sanctity of the Legislative Houses. The counter view to this 
proposal is based on the doctrine that a person is presumed to be innocent 
until he is proved guilty. The Commission is of the view that keeping a person, 
who is accused of serious criminal charges and where the Court is prima facie 
satisfied about his involvement in the crime and consequently framed charges, 
out of electoral arena wo uld be a reasonable restriction in greater public 
interests. There cannot be any grievance on this. However, as a precaution 
against motivated cases by the ruling party, it may be provided that only those 
cases which were filed prior to six months before an election alone would 
lead to disqualification as proposed. It is also suggested that persons found guilty 
by a Commission of Enquiry should also stand disqualified from contesting 
elections. [The provisions in the Jammu & Kashmir Representation of the 
People Act are relevant in this regard] 
In the midst of the recent general elections, the Patna High Court had 
passed an order that persons behind bars cannot contest elections. 
136 

[23 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
On the basis of an application moved by the Election Commission, this Order 
was stayed by the Supreme Court with the observation that the High Court 
could not have passed the Order during the course of the election process. 
However, the SLP [No. 9204-05/2004-ECI vs. Jan Chowkidar (Peoples Watch) 
& Otrs.l is pending before the Supreme Court for final disposal. 
The Commission endorses that the law should be amended as proposed 
above.

Photo Identity Cards 
2045. SHRI R. SHUNMUGASUNDARAM : Will the Minister of LAW 
AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps being taken by the Election Commission of India to 
complete issuance of the Elector Photo Identity Cards (EPIC); and 
(b) the number of voters not issued EPIC so far? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) The Election Commission of India has informed that it has outlined steps to 
complete issue of Elector's Photo Identity Cards in two phases. In the first 
phase, field campaigns for extensive coverage of electors included in the 
existing roll are launched. The campaign is taken up using a targeted approach. 
Parts of electoral roll of a constituency representing groups of small villages or 
parts representing the same village in case of large village, or localities in urban 
areas are clubbed together for the purp oses of this analysis. Locations are 
identified where the residual electors can be photographed—called 
Designated Photography Locations—in such a manner that a team of persons 
is able to cover them in a specified period of time. This campaign mode is 
continued till the threshold level of nearly 85% of the total electors is covered. 
In the second phase, those of the States, who attain the threshold target of 
85% will go into the Maintenance Mode, whereby permanent Designated 
Photography Location centers are provided at the district/sub-divisional 
headquarters. The electors who have either been left out for any reason or those 
electors who are added to the roll later on are required to go to these centers to 
get their cards prepared. It is the end eavour of the Commission to achieve the 
target of issuing the Elector's Photo Identity Cards to all the electors enrolled 
in the electoral roll with respect to 1.1.2005 as qualifying date by the end of 
year 2005. 
(b)The Election Commission has informed that out of 670,097,172 
electors present in the electoral roll with  respect to 1.1.2004 as the qualifying 
date, 205,583,654 electors are without Elector's Photo Identity Cards.
